source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 3 (PDF 46-73, printed 46-73); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 3 (Chemical Bonding), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 The force that holds together two or more atoms, molecules or ions is called a:
blocks.explanation: A chemical bond is the force that holds together two or more atoms, molecules or ions (3.1).

book_ref.quote: A chemical bond is the force that holds together two or more atoms, molecules or ions.

blocks.prompt: 2 Van der Waals forces are usually not termed pure chemical bonds because they are:
blocks.explanation: Being weak enough, van der Waals forces are usually not termed pure chemical bonds (3.1).

book_ref.quote: being weak enough, van der Waals forces are usually not termed as pure chemical bonds

blocks.prompt: 3 According to the Lewis concept, atoms form bonds in order to:

options.text: complete their outermost shells and attain a noble gas-like configuration

blocks.explanation: Atoms make bonds to complete their outermost shells to have a noble gas-like configuration, mostly an octet (3.1).

book_ref.quote: atoms make bonds to complete their outermost shells to have noble gas-like configuration

blocks.prompt: 4 Which statement about NaCl and water is given in the chapter?

options.text: NaCl is covalent and liquid; water is ionic and solid
NaCl is ionic and solid; water is covalent and liquid

blocks.explanation: NaCl has an ionic bond and is solid, but water is a covalent compound and liquid; properties depend on bond type (3.1).

book_ref.quote: NaCl has ionic bond and is solid, but water is a covalent compound and liquid.

blocks.prompt: 5 According to the Lewis theory, an ionic bond is formed by:
blocks.explanation: The ionic bond forms by complete transfer of electrons from an atom of low ionization energy to an atom of high electron affinity (3.1.1).

book_ref.quote: the ionic bond is formed by the complete transfer of electrons from an atom with low ionization energy

blocks.prompt: 6 In ionic bond formation, electrons pass from an atom with low ionization energy to an atom with:
blocks.explanation: Electrons go to the atom with high electron affinity (3.1.1).

book_ref.quote: to another atom with high electron affinity

blocks.prompt: 7 When Na (2, 8, 1) loses one electron, the Na⁺ ion has the electron configuration of:
blocks.explanation: Na⁺ (2, 8) has the configuration of ₁₀Ne, the noble gas nearest to it (3.1.1).

book_ref.quote: which has the electron configuration of ₁₀Ne, a noble gas nearest to it

blocks.prompt: 8 The electron arrangement of the chloride ion Cl⁻ is:
blocks.explanation: Cl (2, 8, 7) gains one electron to form Cl⁻ (2, 8, 8), a noble gas arrangement (3.1.1).

book_ref.quote: Chlorine atom Cl (2, 8, 7) gains one electron to form the chloride ion

blocks.prompt: 9 An ionic bond like that in NaCl is expected between:

options.text: group 1 and 2 metals and group 16 and 17 elements

blocks.explanation: A similar ionic bond is expected between group 1 and 2 metals and groups 16 and 17 elements (3.1.1).

book_ref.quote: A similar type of bond is expected between group 1 and 2 metals and groups 16 and 17 elements.

blocks.prompt: 10 A covalent bond is formed by:

options.text: mutual sharing of electrons between two atoms

blocks.explanation: A covalent bond is formed by the mutual sharing of electrons between two atoms (3.1.2).

book_ref.quote: A covalent bond is formed by the mutual sharing of electrons between two atoms.

blocks.prompt: 11 The bond in the Cl₂ molecule is:
blocks.explanation: The bond between two Cl atoms is purely covalent and non-polar because both atoms have the same electronegativity (3.1.2).

book_ref.quote: The bond between two Cl atoms is purely covalent and non-polar.

blocks.prompt: 12 In a non-polar bond such as Cl–Cl, the bonded atoms:

options.text: carry full positive and negative charges
carry partial charges δ⁺ and δ⁻
remain electrically neutral with no charge on either atom

blocks.explanation: With exactly the same electronegativity, the bonded atoms remain electrically neutral (3.1.2).

book_ref.quote: the bonded atoms remain electrically neutral and there is no charge on either atom

blocks.prompt: 13 Which of the following contains a polar covalent bond?
blocks.explanation: H–Cl, H–Br and H₂O are given as polar covalent; H₂, F₂, Br₂, I₂ are non-polar (3.1.2).

book_ref.quote: Examples of polar covalent bonds are H–Cl, H-Br, H₂O, etc.

blocks.prompt: 14 Which molecule has a non-polar covalent bond like Cl₂?
blocks.explanation: H₂, F₂, Br₂ and I₂ are non-polar like Cl₂ (3.1.2).

book_ref.quote: The other such molecules are H₂, F₂, Br₂ and I₂.

blocks.text: Dative bond (coordinate covalent bond), printed as 3.13

blocks.prompt: 15 A bond in which the shared pair of electrons is donated by only one of the bonding atoms is:
blocks.explanation: A dative (coordinate covalent) bond forms when the shared pair is donated by one of the bonding atoms (3.13).

book_ref.quote: A dative bond is formed between two atoms when the shared pair of electrons is donated by one of the bonding atoms.

blocks.prompt: 16 In the formation of H₃O⁺ from H₂O and H⁺, the donor of the electron pair is:
blocks.explanation: Oxygen donates a lone pair to the electron-deficient proton, forming a dative bond (3.13).

book_ref.quote: the oxygen atom can donate its lone pair of electrons to the acceptor H⁺

blocks.prompt: 17 How many lone pairs of electrons are present on the oxygen atom of a water molecule?
blocks.explanation: H₂O has two covalent bonds and two lone pairs on the O atom (3.13).

book_ref.quote: H₂O has two covalent bonds and there are two lone pairs of electrons on the oxygen atom

blocks.prompt: 18 In carbon monoxide, the dative bond is formed when:

options.text: carbon donates a lone pair to oxygen
carbon transfers two electrons to oxygen
a proton is added to carbon
oxygen donates one of its lone pairs to carbon

blocks.explanation: Carbon needs one more pair to complete its octet; oxygen donates one lone pair, forming a dative bond (3.13).

book_ref.quote: Oxygen atom donates one of its lone pairs for the formation of a covalent bond

blocks.prompt: 19 In the ozone molecule, the central oxygen atom has:

options.text: a double covalent bond on one side and a coordinate covalent bond on the other
a triple bond on one side

blocks.explanation: The central O has three bonds in total: a double covalent bond on one side and a coordinate bond on the other (3.13).

book_ref.quote: the central atom has total three bonds including a double covalent bond on one side

blocks.prompt: 20 In ozone, the oxygen atom that accepts the lone pair carries:
blocks.explanation: The central (donor) O carries a positive charge and the acceptor O a negative charge (3.13).

book_ref.quote: It carries a positive charge, while the oxygen atom that accepts the lone pair carries a negative charge.

blocks.prompt: 21 Which of the following polyatomic ions carries a positive charge?
blocks.explanation: Except the ammonium ion NH₄⁺, the polyatomic ions mentioned mostly carry a negative charge (3.1.4).

book_ref.quote: With the exception of ammonium ion (NH₄⁺), these ions mostly carry a negative charge

blocks.prompt: 22 The correct formula of the nitrate ion is:
blocks.explanation: Nitrate carries one negative charge: N (+5) + 3 × O (−2) = −1, so it is NO₃⁻ (book correction, 3.1.4).

book_ref.quote: The nitrate ion carries one negative charge

blocks.prompt: 23 Which of the following ions is given as an example of an expanded octet?
blocks.explanation: SO₄²⁻, ClO₄⁻ and PO₄³⁻ are prominent examples of expanded octets (3.1.4).

book_ref.quote: the central atom violates the octet rule by expanding its electron density to the higher orbitals

blocks.prompt: 24 How many electrons are present in the valence shell of S in SO₄²⁻?
blocks.explanation: Two double bonds and two single bonds: 2(4) + 2(2) = 12 electrons, 4 more than an octet (3.1.4).

book_ref.quote: Thus, S has 12 electrons in its valence shell and it exceeds the octet by 4 electrons.

blocks.prompt: 25 The expansion of the octet of S in SO₄²⁻ is caused by:

options.text: transfer of electrons to oxygen only
involvement of d orbitals in bonding

blocks.explanation: The d orbital takes part in bonding and accommodates the extra electrons (3.1.4).

book_ref.quote: The expansion of octet is caused by the involvement of the d orbital in bonding

blocks.prompt: 26 When one 3p electron of sulfur moves into a 3d orbital, the number of unpaired electrons becomes:
blocks.explanation: 3s² 3p³ 3d¹ has four unpaired electrons, the state used in SO₂; promoting a 3s electron too gives six (book correction, 3.1.4).

book_ref.quote: Moving one 3p electron into 3d gives four unpaired electrons

blocks.prompt: 27 For the six bonds of sulfur in SO₄²⁻, the excited sulfur atom needs how many unpaired electrons?
blocks.explanation: The six-bond state of S in SO₄²⁻ is 3s¹ 3p³ 3d² with six unpaired electrons (book correction, 3.1.4).

book_ref.quote: which is the state needed for the six bonds of sulfur in SO₄²⁻

blocks.prompt: 28 The central iodine atom of I₃⁻ exceeds the octet by:
blocks.explanation: 2 bonds × 2 + 3 lone pairs × 2 = 10 electrons, so the octet expands by two (3.1.4).

book_ref.quote: has 10 electrons in the valence shell and the octet expands by two electrons

blocks.prompt: 29 The availability of d orbitals in sulfur also explains:

options.text: the zero dipole moment of H₂S
the variable oxidation states of S

blocks.explanation: Extension to more unpaired electrons explains the variable oxidation states of S and its accepting extra electrons (3.1.4).

book_ref.quote: It explains not only the variable oxidation states of S

blocks.prompt: 30 Using the chapter's counting method (2 electrons per single bond), how many electrons surround S in SF₆?
blocks.explanation: SF₆ has six S–F single bonds: 6 × 2 = 12 electrons, an expanded octet (3.1.4, 3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: The Lewis structure of SF₆ is given in Figure 3.19, it shows that this is an AB₆ type molecule.

blocks.prompt: 31 Counting 2 electrons for each bond, by how many electrons does P in PCl₅ exceed the octet?
blocks.explanation: Five P–Cl bonds: 5 × 2 = 10 electrons, i.e. 10 − 8 = 2 more than an octet (3.1.4, 3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: This is evident from the geometry of the PCl₅ molecule given in Figure 3.17.

blocks.text: 3.2 Electronegativity and the type of bond

blocks.prompt: 32 The difference in electronegativity of two bonded atoms gives an approximate measure of:

options.text: bond polarity and the type of bond

blocks.explanation: Electronegativity difference gives an approximate measure of bond polarity and an indication of bond type (3.2).

book_ref.quote: provides an approximate measure of the bond polarity and an indication of the type of bond

blocks.prompt: 33 Two atoms with an electronegativity difference less than 0.4 form a:
blocks.explanation: A difference less than 0.4 means a pure covalent bond (3.2).

book_ref.quote: Two atoms having electronegativity difference less than 0.4 are said to make a pure covalent bond.

blocks.prompt: 34 Electronegativities: N = 3.0 and H = 2.1 (given). The N–H bond is:
blocks.explanation: Difference = 3.0 − 2.1 = 0.9, which lies between 0.4 and 1.8: polar covalent (3.2).

book_ref.quote: An electronegativity difference between 0.4 and 1.8 corresponds to a polar covalent bond

blocks.prompt: 35 Electronegativities: Li = 1.0 and F = 4.0 (given). The bond between Li and F is:
blocks.explanation: Difference = 4.0 − 1.0 = 3.0, above 1.8, so the bond is ionic (3.2).

book_ref.quote: whereas, above this value the bond between two atoms will be ionic in nature

blocks.prompt: 36 The electronegativity difference in NaCl, as given in the chapter, is:
blocks.explanation: The differences for H–H, H–Cl and NaCl are 0, 0.9 and 2.1, respectively (3.2).

book_ref.quote: are 0 (nonpolar), 0.9 (polar covalent), and 2.1 (ionic), respectively

blocks.prompt: 37 Electronegativities: C = 2.5 and Cl = 3.0 (given). The C–Cl bond is:
blocks.explanation: Difference = 3.0 − 2.5 = 0.5, between 0.4 and 1.8: polar covalent (3.2).

book_ref.quote: When this difference is very small or zero, the bond is covalent and nonpolar.

blocks.text: Dipole moment and polarity of molecules

blocks.prompt: 38 A molecule with δ⁺ charge on one part and δ⁻ charge on the other part is called a:
blocks.explanation: Such a molecule is called a dipole and is said to have a dipole moment.

book_ref.quote: A molecule with δ⁺ charge on one part and δ⁻ charge on the other part is called a dipole

blocks.prompt: 39 The unit in which dipole moment is measured is:
blocks.explanation: Dipole moment is measured in Debye units (D); higher dipole moment means higher polarity.

book_ref.quote: Dipole moment is measured in Debye unit (D).

blocks.prompt: 40 In the chapter's convention, the dipole moment of HF is directed:

options.text: in no direction, as it is zero

blocks.explanation: Dipole moments of diatomic molecules are directed from the δ⁺ end to the δ⁻ end, i.e. H to F (Fig. 3.5).

book_ref.quote: are directed from the positive ends (δ⁺) to negative ends (δ⁻)

blocks.prompt: 41 The dipole moment of water given in the chapter is:
blocks.explanation: Water has a dipole moment of 1.85 D directed from the hydrogen end to the oxygen end.

book_ref.quote: The dipole moment of water is 1.85 D

blocks.prompt: 42 The non-zero dipole moment of water shows that the water molecule is:
blocks.explanation: A linear H–O–H would have zero dipole moment; the non-zero value shows water is non-linear.

book_ref.quote: A linear H₂O molecule (H-O-H) would have zero dipole moment.

blocks.prompt: 43 The dipole moment of SO₂ given in the chapter is:
blocks.explanation: SO₂ has a dipole moment of 1.61 D, in the opposite direction to that in water.

book_ref.quote: SO₂ has a dipole moment of 1.61 D

blocks.prompt: 44 CCl₄ is a non-polar molecule although its C–Cl bonds are polar, because:

options.text: C and Cl have the same electronegativity
its four bond moments cancel each other in the perfect tetrahedron
it has two lone pairs on carbon

blocks.explanation: The four C–Cl bond moments are directed so that they cancel; the net dipole moment is zero.

book_ref.quote: The net dipole moment of the CCl₄ molecule is zero making it a non-polar molecule.

blocks.prompt: 45 Which of the following molecules has zero dipole moment because of its trigonal planar symmetry?
blocks.explanation: BF₃ has a symmetrical trigonal planar structure and zero dipole moment.

book_ref.quote: BF₃ has a trigonal planar symmetrical structure and its dipole moment is also zero

blocks.prompt: 46 H₂S has some net dipole moment because:

options.text: it is non-linear, so its polar bond moments do not cancel

blocks.explanation: H₂S is non-linear; its polar bond moments do not cancel, so the molecule has some dipole moment.

book_ref.quote: H₂S is also a non-linear molecule as the individual bonds are polar

blocks.prompt: 47 As a rule, a molecule with the same ligands around the central atom in a regular geometry is:
blocks.explanation: In such molecules individual dipole moments may not be zero, but the overall dipole moment is zero; the molecule is non-polar.

book_ref.quote: the molecules that have same ligands (atoms or groups of atoms with the central atom) in a regular geometry

blocks.text: 3.3.2 Valence shell electron pair repulsion model (VSEPR)

blocks.prompt: 48 The VSEPR model was presented by:
blocks.explanation: The VSEPR model was presented by Sidgwick and Powell in 1940 (3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: This model was presented by Sidgwick and Powell in 1940.

blocks.prompt: 49 The VSEPR model assumes that a molecule takes a shape in which:

options.text: repulsions among the valence electron pairs are minimum

blocks.explanation: A molecule takes a shape such that electronic repulsions among the valence electrons are minimum (3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: a molecule will take a shape such that the electronic repulsions among the valence electrons of that atom are minimum

blocks.prompt: 50 The correct order of repulsions between electron pairs is:
blocks.explanation: Repulsions decrease in the order lp-lp > lp-bp > bp-bp (3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: Lone pair-lone pair (lp-lp) > lone pair-bond pair (lp-bp) > bond pair-bond pair (bp-bp)

blocks.prompt: 51 Lone pairs compress the bond pairs because lone pairs:

options.text: occupy less space than bond pairs
occupy more space than bond pairs

blocks.explanation: Lone-pair electrons occupy more space, so they exert greater repulsion on bond pairs and compress them (3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: The electrons of lone pairs occupy more space than the bond pairs.

blocks.prompt: 52 In the VSEPR model, the two electron pairs of a double bond are regarded as:
blocks.explanation: The pairs of a double or triple bond have higher charge density but are regarded as single pairs (3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: contain a higher electronic charge density, but they are regarded as single pairs

blocks.prompt: 53 To predict a shape, the central atom is mostly chosen as the:

options.text: atom present in the largest number

blocks.explanation: The least electronegative atom, or the element with the least number of atoms, is mostly chosen as central atom (3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: The least electronegative atom or the element with the least number of atoms is mostly selected as the central atom.

blocks.prompt: 54 The actual shape of a molecule (as distinct from its electron pair geometry) is decided by:

options.text: the total number of electron pairs only
the positions of atoms, excluding lone pairs

blocks.explanation: Electron pair geometry depends on total pairs; the actual shape is decided by the atoms excluding lone pairs (3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: Whereas, the actual shape of the molecule is determined by the atoms excluding the lone pairs.

blocks.prompt: 55 BeCl₂ is linear because the two bond pairs around Be are arranged at:
blocks.explanation: Two electron pairs arrange at 180° to minimize repulsion: linear AB₂ (3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: BeCl₂ molecule is of AB₂ type with Be as the central atom and two bond pairs around it

blocks.prompt: 56 Each F–B–F bond angle in BF₃ is:
blocks.explanation: BF₃ is trigonal planar with each F–B–F angle 120° (3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: BF₃ molecule has a trigonal planar shape with each F-B-F bond angle of 120°

blocks.prompt: 57 Which hydride is expected to have a trigonal planar geometry like BF₃?
blocks.explanation: Similar geometries are expected in group 3 (III-A) hydrides: AlH₃, GaH₃, BH₃ (3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: The similar geometries are expected in the hydrides of group 3 (III-A)

blocks.prompt: 58 The shape of SnCl₂ (in the vapour phase) is:

options.text: v-shaped with bond angle less than 120°

blocks.explanation: Sn makes two bonds and keeps one lone pair; the shape is v-shaped with angle less than 120° (3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: The actual shape of SnCl₂ is v-shaped and bond angle less than 120°

blocks.prompt: 59 Which molecule has all three regions around the central atom occupied by double bonds and a perfectly trigonal structure?
blocks.explanation: In SO₃ all three regions are S=O bonds; the structure is perfectly trigonal with 120° angles (3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: The structure of SO₃ is perfectly trigonal with each angle equal to 120°.

blocks.prompt: 60 SO₂ is angular because:

options.text: one corner of the triangle is a lone pair and two corners are S=O bonds
its two S=O bonds are at 180°

blocks.explanation: In SO₂ one corner of the triangle holds a lone pair, so the molecule is angular like SnCl₂ (3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: one corner of the triangle is occupied by a lone pair and the other two corners each by a double bond

blocks.prompt: 61 A tetrahedral shape has how many bond angles?
blocks.explanation: A tetrahedron has four corners, four faces, six edges and six bond angles (3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: The tetrahedral shape has four corners, four faces, six edges and six bond angles.

blocks.prompt: 62 Each H–C–H bond angle in methane is:
blocks.explanation: The four bonded pairs point to the corners of a regular tetrahedron; each angle is 109.5° (3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: Each H-C-H bond angle is perfectly 109.5°.

blocks.prompt: 63 The bond angle in NH₃ is reduced from 109.5° to:
blocks.explanation: The lone pair on N reduces the ideal angle 109.5° to 107° (3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: Due to a lone pairs the ideal angle 109.5° is reduced to 107°

blocks.prompt: 64 The bond angle in NF₃ is:
blocks.explanation: Three highly electronegative F atoms compress the angles of NF₃ to 102.5° (3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: The bond angles are further compressed to 102.5°.

blocks.prompt: 65 One reason the bond angle of NF₃ is smaller than that of NH₃ is that the N–F bond pairs:

options.text: lie closer to the N atom
lie closer to F atoms, so their mutual repulsions are weaker

blocks.explanation: N–F bond pairs are closer to F; the increased distance weakens their repulsions so the bonds come closer (3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: The increased distances in these bond pairs make their repulsions weaker and allow the bonds to come closer.

blocks.prompt: 66 The bond angle in the water molecule is:
blocks.explanation: Two lone pairs repel more strongly, reducing the angle of H₂O to 104.5° (3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: due to the greater repulsions of the lone pairs, the bond angle is reduced to 104.5°

blocks.prompt: 67 The shape of the hydronium ion H₃O⁺ is:
blocks.explanation: H₃O⁺ is AB₄ type with one lone pair, trigonal pyramidal like NH₃ (3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: possesses a trigonal pyramidal shape just like the ammonia molecule

blocks.prompt: 68 The shape of the amide ion [NH₂]⁻ is:
blocks.explanation: [NH₂]⁻ has two lone pairs and two bond pairs: tetrahedral geometry but bent shape like water (3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: The amide ion [NH₂]⁻ is also AB₄ type as it is surrounded by two lone pairs and two bond pairs.

blocks.prompt: 69 In PCl₅, the angle between an axial atom and a planar atom is:
blocks.explanation: In the trigonal bipyramid, angles in the plane are 120° and axial-to-planar angles are 90° (3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: The angles within the plane are 120° and that between the axial atom and a planar atom is 90°.

blocks.prompt: 70 The central iodine atom of I₃⁻ has:

options.text: five bond pairs and no lone pair
three bond pairs and two lone pairs
two bond pairs and three lone pairs
two bond pairs and two lone pairs

blocks.explanation: Five pairs around I: two bond pairs and three lone pairs (3.3.2; book correction to Table 3.1).

book_ref.quote: There are five electron pairs around the iodine atom including two bond pairs and three lone pairs.

blocks.prompt: 71 The actual shape of the tri-iodide ion [I₃]⁻ is:
blocks.explanation: Excluding the three equatorial lone pairs, the I atoms lie on the axis at 180°: linear (3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: the actual shape of the tri-iodide ion is linear and the iodine atoms are farthest apart at an angle of 180°

blocks.prompt: 72 In I₃⁻, the three lone pairs occupy:

options.text: the corners of the trigonal (planar) region
one apex and two planar corners
positions at 90° to each other only

blocks.explanation: The lone pairs occupy the trigonal region and the I atoms occur on the apices above and below the plane (3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: The lone pairs occupy the corners of the trigonal region and the iodine atoms occur on the apices

blocks.prompt: 73 All the A–B–A angles in an octahedral (AB₆) molecule are:
blocks.explanation: In octahedral geometry four pairs form a square and two lie on a perpendicular axis; all angles are 90° (3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: All the ABA angles in this type of geometry are of 90°.

blocks.prompt: 74 The actual shape of XeF₄ is:
blocks.explanation: XeF₄ has four bond pairs and two lone pairs at 180°; its shape is square planar with F–Xe–F angles of 90° (3.3.2, book correction).

book_ref.quote: XeF₄ is an AB₆ type molecule with four bond pairs and two lone pairs.

blocks.prompt: 75 In XeF₄, the two lone pairs are at an angle of:
blocks.explanation: The two lone pairs stay farthest apart, at 180° (3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: The two lone pairs remain at farthest distance at angle of 180°.

blocks.prompt: 76 Which species has 5 electron pairs, 3 lone pairs and a linear shape?
blocks.explanation: I₃⁻ belongs to 5 pairs and 3 lone pairs (book correction to Table 3.1); BeCl₂ is linear with only 2 pairs.

book_ref.quote: I₃⁻ belongs in a row with 5 electron pairs and 3 lone pairs.

blocks.prompt: 77 Which pair shows the same electron pair geometry (tetrahedral) but different shapes?
blocks.explanation: CH₄ and H₂O both have four electron pairs (tetrahedral geometry) but CH₄ is tetrahedral and H₂O is v-shaped (Table 3.1).

book_ref.quote: For example, CCl₄ has total four electron pairs and its geometry is tetrahedral.

blocks.prompt: 78 Highly electronegative atoms attached to the central atom cause:

options.text: weaker bond pair repulsions but stronger lone pair repulsion

blocks.explanation: Highly electronegative atoms decrease repulsions between bond pairs but increase repulsion by the lone pair (3.3.2).

book_ref.quote: results in decreased electronic repulsions between the bond pairs, but stronger repulsion by the lone pair

blocks.text: 3.3.3 Applications of the VSEPR model in drug designing

blocks.prompt: 79 Chemical substances that prevent, diagnose or treat a disease are called:
blocks.explanation: Drugs are chemical substances that prevent, diagnose or treat a disease (3.3.3).

book_ref.quote: Drugs are chemical substances that prevent, diagnose, or treat a disease.

blocks.prompt: 80 A receptor is mostly a:

options.text: protein that receives and responds to a ligand by binding

blocks.explanation: A receptor is mostly a protein that receives and responds to a ligand through binding (3.3.3).

book_ref.quote: A receptor is mostly a protein that receives and responds to a ligand through binding.

blocks.prompt: 81 The feature by which each drug interacts with a specific target to a different degree is called:
blocks.explanation: This feature is called specificity of a drug or a ligand (3.3.3).

book_ref.quote: this feature is called specificity of a drug or a ligand

blocks.prompt: 82 Only ligands with a suitable shape fit the active site of a target, just as:

options.text: a specific key fits a specific lock

blocks.explanation: Ligands of suitable shape fit the active sites as a specific key fits a specific lock (3.3.3).

book_ref.quote: Only the ligands with suitable shape can fit in the active sites of a biological target

blocks.prompt: 83 Aspirin blocks the enzyme COX by binding to its active site through its:
blocks.explanation: Aspirin binds to the active site of COX (cyclooxygenase) through the acetyl group (–OCCH₃) (3.3.3).

book_ref.quote: It interacts with an enzyme COX (cyclooxygenase) by binding to its active site through the acetyl group

blocks.prompt: 84 Aspirin is described in the chapter as:
blocks.explanation: Aspirin is an analgesic (painkiller) used for relief from pain (3.3.3).

book_ref.quote: Aspirin is an analgesic drug (painkiller)

blocks.prompt: 85 A limitation of the VSEPR model, which VBT removes, is that VSEPR:

options.text: does not give reasons for the formation of bonds

blocks.explanation: VSEPR explains shapes but not why bonds form; VBT deals with both bond formation and shapes (3.4).

book_ref.quote: The VSEPR model predicts and explains the shapes of molecules but does not give reasons for the formation of bonds.

blocks.prompt: 86 According to VBT, a covalent bond forms when:

options.text: half-filled valence orbitals of similar energy on two atoms overlap

blocks.explanation: A covalent bond forms when half-filled valence orbitals of two atoms with similar energy overlap (3.4).

book_ref.quote: A covalent bond is formed when half-filled orbitals in the valence shells of two atoms with similar energy overlap.

blocks.prompt: 87 According to VBT, a greater overlap of orbitals gives:
blocks.explanation: A greater overlap of the orbitals results in a stronger bond (3.4).

book_ref.quote: A greater overlap of the orbitals results in a stronger bond.

blocks.prompt: 88 Covalent bonds are directional; their direction is decided by:

options.text: the shape and mode of the overlapping orbitals

blocks.explanation: The direction of the bond is determined by the shape and mode of overlapping orbitals (3.4).

book_ref.quote: The direction of the bond is determined by the shape and mode of the overlapping orbitals.

blocks.prompt: 89 A sigma bond is formed by:

options.text: sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals

blocks.explanation: A sigma bond forms by linear overlap of two half-filled orbitals on the nuclear axis (3.4.1).

book_ref.quote: A sigma bond is formed by the linear overlap of two half-filled atomic orbitals on adjacent atoms.

blocks.prompt: 90 The s-s overlap is seen in the formation of:
blocks.explanation: In H₂ each H atom has a half-filled s orbital; they overlap s-s (3.4.1).

book_ref.quote: This type of overlap occurs during the formation of the H₂ molecule

blocks.prompt: 91 In HCl, the sigma bond is formed by:
blocks.explanation: A half-filled s orbital of H overlaps with a half-filled p orbital of Cl (3.4.1).

book_ref.quote: a half-filled s orbital of hydrogen overlaps with a half-filled p orbital of chlorine

blocks.prompt: 92 HCl is a polar molecule because the electron density is higher:
blocks.explanation: Electron density is higher near Cl because of its higher electronegativity, making HCl polar (3.4.1).

book_ref.quote: The electron density is higher close to the Cl atom due to its higher electronegativity value.

blocks.prompt: 93 In Cl₂ formed by p-p overlap, the electron density is symmetrical around both nuclei because:

options.text: one atom donates a lone pair
both atoms have the same electronegativity

blocks.explanation: Both Cl atoms have the same electronegativity, so the electron density is symmetrical (3.4.1).

book_ref.quote: The electron density is symmetrical around the nuclei of the two Cl atoms

blocks.prompt: 94 The bond angle in H₂S is:
blocks.explanation: Two 3p orbitals of S overlap with 1s of two H atoms, giving a v-shaped molecule with 92° (3.4.1).

book_ref.quote: A v-shaped molecule is thus formed having a bond angle of 92°

blocks.prompt: 95 According to the chapter, the H–S–H angle (92°) is smaller than the H–O–H angle (104.5°) because:

options.text: S is more electronegative than O
the orbitals of S are larger and the lone pair exerts a stronger repulsion

blocks.explanation: The Interesting Information box gives: the orbitals of S are larger and the lone pair exerts a stronger repulsion (3.4.1).

book_ref.quote: This is because the orbitals of S are larger and the lone pair exerts a stronger repulsion.

blocks.prompt: 96 A π bond is formed by:

options.text: parallel (sideways) overlap of p orbitals above and below the nuclear plane

blocks.explanation: Parallel p orbitals overlap with lobes above and below the plane of the nuclei, forming a π bond (3.4.1).

book_ref.quote: They overlap in a parallel way so that the two p lobes overlap above the plane of the nuclei

blocks.prompt: 97 The double bond in O₂ (VBT) consists of:

options.text: one σ bond and one π bond
one σ bond and two π bonds

blocks.explanation: Linear px overlap gives σ and parallel py overlap gives π; O atoms are doubly bonded through σ and π (3.4.1).

book_ref.quote: The oxygen atoms are doubly bonded through σ and π bonds.

blocks.text: 3.5 Atomic orbital hybridization and shapes of molecules

blocks.prompt: 98 Mixing of atomic orbitals of slightly different energies and shapes to form a new set of equivalent orbitals is called:
blocks.explanation: This process is called hybridization (3.5).

book_ref.quote: are mixed together to form a new set of equivalent orbitals of same energy and same shape is called hybridization

blocks.prompt: 99 If one s and two p orbitals mix, the number of hybrid orbitals formed is:
blocks.explanation: The number of mixing orbitals always equals the number of hybrid orbitals: 1 + 2 = 3 (3.5).

book_ref.quote: The number of mixing orbitals is always equal to the number of the resulting hybrid orbitals.

blocks.prompt: 100 Hybridization involves mixing of orbitals:

options.text: of a metal and a non-metal

blocks.explanation: Hybridization is the mixing of orbitals in a single atom or ion (3.5).

book_ref.quote: Hybridization is a process of mixing of orbitals in a single atom (or ion).

blocks.prompt: 101 Which orbitals can be mixed to form hybrid orbitals?

options.text: only orbitals of comparable (relatively close) energies

blocks.explanation: Only orbitals of comparable energies can be mixed (3.5).

book_ref.quote: Only orbitals of comparable (relatively close) energies can be mixed to form hybrid orbitals.

blocks.prompt: 102 In sp³ hybridization, the number of hybrid orbitals formed is:
blocks.explanation: One s and three p orbitals intermix to give four sp³ hybrid orbitals of the same energy and shape (3.5.1).

book_ref.quote: intermix to give a new set of four orbitals of same energy and same shape

blocks.prompt: 103 The sp³ hybrid orbitals are arranged in a:
blocks.explanation: sp³ hybrid orbitals are arranged tetrahedrally, as in CH₄ (3.5.1).

book_ref.quote: These hybrid orbitals are arranged in the tetrahedral geometry

blocks.prompt: 104 Each sp³ hybrid orbital consists of:

options.text: two lobes, one larger and one smaller

blocks.explanation: Each sp³ hybrid orbital has two lobes, one larger and one smaller; the small lobe is usually not shown (3.5.1).

book_ref.quote: Each sp³ hybrid orbital consists of two lobes, one larger and the other smaller.

blocks.prompt: 105 The C–H bonds in methane result from:
blocks.explanation: Four sp³ hybrid orbitals of C overlap with 1s orbitals of four H atoms: sp³-s sigma bonds (3.5.1).

book_ref.quote: The four C-H bonds, which result from sp³-s overlaps

blocks.prompt: 106 The angle between sp² hybrid orbitals is:
blocks.explanation: Three sp² hybrid orbitals are trigonal planar at 120° (3.5.1).

book_ref.quote: The three half-filled sp² hybrid orbitals are arranged in a trigonal planar geometry with bond angles of 120°.

blocks.prompt: 107 In BF₃, the B–F bonds are formed by the overlap of:

options.text: sp³ orbitals of B with 2s orbitals of F
sp orbitals of B with 1s orbitals of F
sp² orbitals of B with 2p orbitals of F
2s orbitals of B with 2s orbitals of F

blocks.explanation: Three half-filled sp² orbitals of B overlap with half-filled 2pz orbitals of three F atoms (3.5.1).

book_ref.quote: BF₃ is formed by the overlap of three half-filled sp² hybrid orbitals of boron with 2pz orbitals of three fluorine atoms

blocks.prompt: 108 The sp hybrid orbitals are oriented at:
blocks.explanation: Two sp hybrid orbitals lie in a linear geometry at 180° (3.5.1).

book_ref.quote: These sp hybrid orbitals are arranged in linear geometry and oriented at 180°.

blocks.prompt: 109 The hybridization of Be in BeCl₂ is:
blocks.explanation: BeCl₂ forms when two sp hybrid orbitals of Be overlap with half-filled p orbitals of Cl (3.5.1).

book_ref.quote: It is formed when two sp hybrid orbitals of Be atom overlap with the half-filled p-orbitals of chlorine atoms.

blocks.prompt: 110 Which molecule's planar geometry is explained by sp² hybridization?
blocks.explanation: sp² hybridization explains the planar geometry of BF₃ (3.5.1).

book_ref.quote: The sp² hybridization explains the geometry of planar molecules such as BF₃.

blocks.prompt: 111 In sp hybridization, the orbitals that intermix are:

options.text: one s and two p orbitals
one s and three p orbitals
one s and one p orbital

blocks.explanation: One s and one p orbital intermix to give two sp hybrid orbitals (3.5.1).

book_ref.quote: one s (low energy and spherical) and one p orbital (high energy and dumb-bell shaped)

blocks.prompt: 112 According to MOT, molecular orbitals are:
blocks.explanation: Atomic orbitals overlap to form molecular orbitals, which are characteristic of the whole molecule (3.6).

book_ref.quote: which are characteristic of the whole molecule

blocks.prompt: 113 How many molecular orbitals are formed when two atomic orbitals overlap?
blocks.explanation: Two atomic orbitals overlap to form two molecular orbitals, one bonding and one anti-bonding (3.6).

book_ref.quote: Two atomic orbitals overlap to form two molecular orbitals.

blocks.prompt: 114 When atomic orbitals of opposite signs overlap, they form:

options.text: a bonding molecular orbital of lower energy
an anti-bonding molecular orbital of higher energy

blocks.explanation: Same-sign overlap gives a lower-energy bonding MO; opposite signs give a higher-energy anti-bonding MO (3.6).

book_ref.quote: high energy anti-bonding molecular orbital (σ* or π*) is formed

blocks.prompt: 115 A diatomic species has 8 bonding electrons and 2 anti-bonding electrons. Its bond order is:

book_ref.quote: is taken as half of the difference between the number of bonding electrons

blocks.prompt: 116 In H₂, the bonding molecular orbital is:

options.text: located only on one H atom

blocks.explanation: The bonding MO is symmetrical about the nuclear axis; the anti-bonding MO has its electron density away from the nuclei (3.6).

book_ref.quote: the anti-bonding molecular orbital has the electron density away from the nuclei

blocks.prompt: 117 In MOT, the two lobes of a p orbital are given:

options.text: opposite signs (+ and −) of the wave function

blocks.explanation: One lobe of a p orbital is given '+' and the other '−'; overlap takes place between lobes of suitable sign (3.6).

book_ref.quote: For example, one lobe of a p orbital is given the

blocks.prompt: 118 Head-on approach of two 2px orbitals gives:

options.text: σ(2px) bonding and σ*(2px) anti-bonding MOs

blocks.explanation: p orbitals approaching along the same axis give σ(2px) and σ*(2px) molecular orbitals (3.6).

book_ref.quote: This combination of atomic orbitals gives rise to σ (2px) bonding and σ* (2px) antibonding molecular orbitals.

blocks.prompt: 119 The bonding molecular orbitals π(2py) and π(2pz) have:

options.text: maximum electron density on the nuclear axis
zero electron density on the nuclear axis

blocks.explanation: The π bonding MOs have zero electron density on the nuclear axis, called the nodal plane (3.6).

book_ref.quote: have zero electron density on the nuclear axis (called the nodal plane)

blocks.prompt: 120 π molecular orbitals are formed when two p orbitals interact with their axes:
blocks.explanation: When the axes of py or pz orbitals are parallel, they interact sideways to form π MOs (3.6).

book_ref.quote: When the axes of two p-orbitals (i.e py or pz orbitals) are parallel to each other

blocks.text: 3.6.1 Molecular orbital diagrams of some diatomic molecules and their bond orders

blocks.prompt: 121 He₂ molecule is not formed because its bond order is:
blocks.explanation: Two electrons in σ1s and two in σ*1s: bond order (2 − 2)/2 = 0, so He₂ is not formed (3.6.1).

book_ref.quote: But on calculation we discover that the bond order for He₂ is zero.

blocks.prompt: 122 From its MO diagram, the bond order of N₂ (counting the 2p electrons: 6 bonding, 0 anti-bonding) is:
blocks.explanation: Bond order = (6 − 0)/2 = 3, so N₂ has a triple bond (3.6.1).

book_ref.quote: Nitrogen molecule has a triple bond between its atoms.

blocks.prompt: 123 In the energy order of N₂ molecular orbitals, the highest-energy orbital is:
blocks.explanation: σ2s < σ*2s < π2py = π2pz < σ2px < π*2py = π*2pz < σ*2px (3.6.1, book correction).

book_ref.quote: it is the anti-bonding σ*2px orbital

blocks.prompt: 124 A paramagnetic substance is one that:

options.text: is repelled by an electric field
is attracted by a magnetic field

blocks.explanation: Paramagnetic means attracted by a magnetic field; such substances have one or more unpaired electrons (3.6.1).

book_ref.quote: Oxygen molecule is paramagnetic in nature, which means it is attracted by a magnetic field.

blocks.prompt: 125 The number of unpaired electrons in an O₂ molecule according to MOT is:
blocks.explanation: O₂ has two unpaired electrons, one each in π*(2py) and π*(2pz) (3.6.1).

book_ref.quote: The MO diagram of oxygen shows the presence of two unpaired electrons

blocks.prompt: 126 A substance is strongly paramagnetic when it has:

options.text: a large number of unpaired electrons

blocks.explanation: A substance with a large number of unpaired electrons is strongly paramagnetic (3.6.1).

book_ref.quote: A substance with large number of unpaired electrons is strongly paramagnetic.

blocks.prompt: 127 Liquid oxygen gets suspended between the poles of a strong magnet because O₂ is:
blocks.explanation: Unpaired electrons give O₂ a net magnetic field; it is paramagnetic and is attracted by the magnet (3.6.1).

book_ref.quote: Liquid oxygen is attracted and gets suspended between the poles of a strong magnet.

blocks.prompt: 128 The bond order of O₂ according to MOT is:
blocks.explanation: Bond order of O₂ = (6 − 2)/2 = 2: one σ and one π bond (3.6.1).

book_ref.quote: MOT successfully explains the paramagnetic behavior of oxygen molecule.

blocks.prompt: 129 Two 1s orbitals of He atoms combine to give:
blocks.explanation: Two 1s orbitals give bonding σ1s and anti-bonding σ*1s; the print's δ is a misprint for σ (3.6.1, book correction).

book_ref.quote: Two 1s orbitals give the bonding σ1s and the anti-bonding σ*1s molecular orbitals

blocks.prompt: 130 Compared with chemical bonds, the attraction between molecules is:
blocks.explanation: The attraction between molecules is much weaker than chemical bonds (3.7).

book_ref.quote: However, the attraction between the molecules is much weaker than the chemical bonds.

blocks.prompt: 131 Instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces are also called:
blocks.explanation: Instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces are London dispersion forces (3.7).

book_ref.quote: Instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces or London dispersion forces

blocks.prompt: 132 Van der Waals forces mainly give substances their particular:
blocks.explanation: These forces bring molecules close together and give particular physical properties in gas, liquid and solid states (3.7).

book_ref.quote: give particular physical properties to the substances in gaseous, liquid, and solid states

blocks.prompt: 133 The average amount of energy required to break all bonds of a particular type in one mole of a substance is:
blocks.explanation: This is the definition of bond energy; its unit is kJ mol⁻¹ (3.9).

book_ref.quote: The bond energy is the average amount of energy required to break all bonds of a particular type in one mole of a substance.

blocks.prompt: 134 Among H–F, H–Cl, H–Br and H–I, the bond with the highest bond energy is:
blocks.explanation: Bond energy rises with electronegativity difference: H–F 565 kJ mol⁻¹ is highest, H–I 295 lowest (3.9).

book_ref.quote: This is why the bond energy for HF is higher (565 kJ mol⁻¹) than for HI (295 kJ mol⁻¹).

blocks.prompt: 135 Bond energy of H–X bonds rises with electronegativity difference because greater polarity:

options.text: adds an additional attractive force between the atoms

blocks.explanation: Greater electronegativity difference gives greater polarity, adding attractive force that binds the atoms (3.9).

book_ref.quote: the bond polarity also becomes greater and this gives rise to additional attractive force

blocks.prompt: 136 Using Table 3.2, how much more energy does a C≡C bond have than a C=C bond?
blocks.explanation: C≡C − C=C = 839 − 614 = 225 kJ mol⁻¹; multiple bonds are stronger: C≡C > C=C > C–C (3.9).

book_ref.quote: It may be noted that energies of multiple bonds are greater than those of single bonds

blocks.prompt: 137 Using the C–H bond energy 413 kJ mol⁻¹ (Table 3.2), the energy needed to break all C–H bonds in 2 mol of CH₄ is:
blocks.explanation: 2 mol CH₄ contain 2 × 4 = 8 mol C–H bonds: 8 × 413 = 3304 kJ (3.9).

book_ref.quote: The bond energies/enthalpies of some bonds are presented in Table 3.2.

blocks.prompt: 138 Using Table 3.2, the weakest bond among the following is:
blocks.explanation: Bond energy measures bond strength; I–I has the lowest value, 149 kJ mol⁻¹ (Table 3.2).

book_ref.quote: Bond energy is a measure of the strength of a bond and its reactivity.

blocks.prompt: 139 The distance between the nuclei of two atoms forming a covalent bond is called:
blocks.explanation: This is the definition of bond length (3.9).

book_ref.quote: Bond length is the distance between the nuclei of two atoms forming a covalent bond.

blocks.prompt: 140 Bond lengths are determined experimentally by:

options.text: measuring the heat of a reaction
electron diffraction, X-ray diffraction or spectral studies

blocks.explanation: Bond lengths are found by physical techniques: electron diffraction, X-ray diffraction or spectral studies (3.9).

book_ref.quote: such as electron diffraction, X-ray diffraction, or spectral studies

blocks.prompt: 141 From Table 3.3, which bond is the longest?
blocks.explanation: Bond length increases with atom size: C–F 135 < C–Cl 180 < C–Br 196 < C–I 214 pm (3.9).

book_ref.quote: With an increase in size of the atoms, the covalent bond length also increases.

blocks.prompt: 142 Covalent radii: C = 77 pm and F = 64 pm (given). The expected C–F length is 141 pm, but Table 3.3 gives 135 pm. The shortening is due to:

options.text: a π bond between C and F
ionic character from the electronegativity difference

blocks.explanation: 77 + 64 = 141 pm; the observed 135 pm is 6 pm shorter. Electronegativity difference gives ionic character, whose extra attraction shortens the bond (3.9).

book_ref.quote: The ionic character results in shortening of the bond length

blocks.prompt: 143 The Si–F bond length calculated from covalent radii (Si = 117 pm, F = 64 pm) is:
blocks.explanation: 117 + 64 = 181 pm, while the observed Si–F length in SiF₄ is near 155 pm (3.9).

book_ref.quote: whereas the calculation of Si-F bond from the covalent radii of Si and F (Si=117 pm and F=64 pm) is 181 pm

blocks.prompt: 144 From Table 3.3, the correct order of carbon-carbon bond lengths is:
blocks.explanation: C–C 154 pm, C=C 133 pm, C≡C 120 pm: the nature of the bond (single, double, triple) affects bond length (3.9).

book_ref.quote: The bond length of a bond is governed by many factors including electronegativity, size

blocks.text: 3.10 A comparison among ionic, covalent, metallic bonds and intermolecular forces

blocks.prompt: 145 According to Table 3.4, the strongest of the following is:
blocks.explanation: Ionic bond in NaCl 760 kJ mol⁻¹ > O–H 464 > hydrogen bonding > dipole forces > van der Waals (3.10).

book_ref.quote: The bond energy of ionic bond (sodium chloride, 760 kJ mol⁻¹) is highest

blocks.prompt: 146 Chemical bonds differ from intermolecular forces because chemical bonds:

options.text: form new species through transfer and sharing of electrons

blocks.explanation: Chemical bonds form new species through transfer and sharing of electrons; intermolecular forces bring molecules closer and influence physical properties (3.10).

book_ref.quote: Firstly, chemical bonds result in the formation of new species through transfer and sharing of electrons.

blocks.prompt: 147 The strength of a bond or force is measured by its:
blocks.explanation: The distinctive feature is strength, which is measured by bond energy (3.10).

book_ref.quote: The distinctive feature of the chemical bonds and intermolecular forces is their bond strength.

blocks.prompt: 148 The average bond energy of the metallic bond given in the chapter is:
blocks.explanation: The metallic bond (100-150 kJ mol⁻¹) is weaker than both ionic and covalent bonds (3.10).

book_ref.quote: The average bond energy of the metallic bond is 100-150 kJ mol⁻¹.

blocks.prompt: 149 The low strength of the metallic bond is explained by:

options.text: extensive delocalization of electrons in the metallic crystal

blocks.explanation: A satisfactory argument is the extensive delocalization of electrons within the metallic crystal (3.10).

book_ref.quote: A satisfactory argument for the low strength of metallic bond is extensive delocalization of electrons

blocks.prompt: 150 The range of energies of permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces in Table 3.4 is:
blocks.explanation: Permanent dipole-dipole forces are 5-20 kJ mol⁻¹, weaker than hydrogen bonding (3.10).

book_ref.quote: The permanent dipole-dipole forces (5-20 kJ mol⁻¹)
